nodes.name: Total complex of a sequence of complexes
nodes.statement: If $A_0^{\bullet}\to\ldots \to A_n^{\bullet}$ is a sequence of maps (with $f_i:A_i\to A_{i+1}$ )of complex such that the composition of two consecutive maps is $0$, then let's denote $[A_0^{\bullet}\to\ldots \to A_n^{\bullet-n}]$ the total complex of this double complex, defined by the following data:\begin{itemize} \item The object in degré $k$ is $\bigoplus\limits_{i=0}^n A_i[-i]^k$ \item The diferential is given by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} d_{A_0} & 0 & \ldots & \ldots & 0\\ f_0 & -d_{A_1} & \ldots & \ldots & 0\\ 0 & f_1 & \ldots & \ldots & 0\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & & \vdots\\ \vdots & \vdots & & (-1)^{n-1}d_{A_{n-1}} & 0\\ 0 & 0 & \ldots & f_{n-1} & (-1)^nd_{A_n}\\ \end{pmatrix}$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Total complex of a chain of complex maps with zero consecutive composites: degree-$k$ object $\bigoplus_i A_i[-i]^k$, differential the lower-bidiagonal matrix of $\pm d_{A_i}$ and $f_i$.
nodes.label: def:total_complex

nodes.name: Proof that the total complex differential squares to zero
nodes.statement: One needs to check that the matrix square is $0$. Let $M$ be this matrix and $(i,j)$ be integers. \[M^2[i,j]=\sum\limits_{k=1}^n M[i,k]M[k,j]= M[i,i] M[i,j]+M[i,i-1]M[i-1,j]\] One can distinguish four cases:\begin{itemize} \item If $j$ is not in $\{i-2,i-1,i,\}$ then the two terms are $0$. \item If $j=i$, then $M^2[i,j]=((-1)^i d_{A_i})^2+0=0$. \item If $j=i-1$ then $M^2[i,j]0+(-1)^i d_{A_i}\circ f_i+ (-1)^{i+1}d_{A_{i+1}}\circ f_i=0$ because $f_i$ is a morphism of complex. \item If $j=i-2$ then $M^2[i,j]=f_{i}\circ f_{i-1}=0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation of $M^2[i,j]$ by case analysis on $j\in\{i,i-1,i-2\}$ versus other indices.

nodes.name: Reduce to $M^2=0$ and expand $M^2[i,j]$ as two terms
nodes.statement:

    \[M^2[i,j]=\sum\limits_{k=1}^n M[i,k]M[k,j]= M[i,i] M[i,j]+M[i,i-1]M[i-1,j]\]

    One can distinguish four cases:
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $M^2=0$ and expand $M^2[i,j]$ as two terms.

nodes.name: Case $j\notin\{i-2,i-1,i\}$: both terms vanish
nodes.statement: If $j$ is not in $\{i-2,i-1,i,\}$ then the two terms are $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $j\notin\{i-2,i-1,i\}$: both terms vanish.

nodes.statement: If $j=i-1$ then $M^2[i,j]0+(-1)^i d_{A_i}\circ f_i+ (-1)^{i+1}d_{A_{i+1}}\circ f_i=0$ because $f_i$ is a morphism of complex.
nodes.statement_short: Case $j=i-1$: $f_i$ commutes with differentials.

nodes.statement: If $j=i-2$ then $M^2[i,j]=f_{i}\circ f_{i-1}=0$.

nodes.name: Cone as a total complex
nodes.statement: In particular, if $f:A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet}$ is a morphism of complex then $[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}]$ is the cone of the morphism f.

nodes.name: Quasi-isomorphism iff cone acyclic
nodes.statement: A morphism of complex $f:A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet}$ is a quasi isomorphism if and only if, its cone is acyclic.
assumptions: A morphism of complex $f:A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet}$
conclusions: is a quasi isomorphism if and only if, its cone is acyclic
nodes.label: lem:q-iso_iff_cone_acyclic

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: One get's a short exact sequence $0\to B^{\bullet}[-1]\to [A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}]\to A^{\bullet} \to 0$ by using the canonical inclusion and projection over the direct sum. The long exact sequence induced in cohomology is then: \[\ldots H^{k-1}A^{\bullet} \to H^k B^{\bullet}[-1]\to H^k[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}]\to H^k A^{\bullet}\to H^{k+1}B^{\bullet}[-1]\ldots\] By using the fact that $H^k B^{\bullet}[-1]=H^{k-1}B^{\bullet}$ one gets: \[\ldots\to H^{k-1} A^{\bullet} \to H^{k-1} B^{\bullet}\to H^k[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}]\to H^k A^{\bullet}\to H^kB^{\bullet}\ldots\] And then the statement is straightforward by reading the exact sequence.
nodes.statement_short: Long exact cohomology sequence of the cone's short exact sequence $0\to B[-1]\to\mathrm{Cone}\to A\to 0$; read off the equivalence.

nodes.name: Short exact sequence of the cone
nodes.statement:
One get's a short exact sequence $0\to B^{\bullet}[-1]\to [A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}]\to A^{\bullet} \to 0$
    by using the canonical inclusion and projection over the direct sum.
nodes.statement_short: Short exact sequence of the cone.

nodes.name: Induced long exact sequence in cohomology
nodes.statement: The long exact sequence induced in cohomology is then: \[\ldots H^{k-1}A^{\bullet} \to H^k B^{\bullet}[-1]\to H^k[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}]\to H^k A^{\bullet}\to H^{k+1}B^{\bullet}[-1]\ldots\]
nodes.statement_short: Induced long exact sequence in cohomology.

nodes.name: Rewrite with the shift and conclude from exactness
nodes.statement:
By using the fact that $H^k B^{\bullet}[-1]=H^{k-1}B^{\bullet}$ one gets:  \[\ldots\to  H^{k-1} A^{\bullet} \to H^{k-1} B^{\bullet}\to H^k[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}]\to H^k A^{\bullet}\to H^kB^{\bullet}\ldots\]

    And then the statement is straightforward by reading the exact sequence.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite with the shift and conclude from exactness.

nodes.name: Acyclic three-term total complex gives a long exact sequence
nodes.statement: If a complex $[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}\to C^{\bullet-2}]$ is acyclic then there is a long exact sequence \[\ldots \to H^k A\to H^k B\to H^k C\to \ldots\]
assumptions: a complex $[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}\to C^{\bullet-2}]$ is acyclic
conclusions: there is a long exact sequence \[\ldots \to H^k A\to H^k B\to H^k C\to \ldots\]
nodes.label: lem:complex_total_of_three_is_acyclic

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: One can see that by construction there is a canonical isomorphism of complexess: $[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}\to C^{\bullet-2}]=[A^{\bullet}\to [B^{\bullet}\to C^{\bullet-1}]^{\bullet-1}]$. Then by the previous lemma: $A^{\bullet}\to [B^{\bullet}\to C^{\bullet-1}]$ is a quasi isomorphism. One can then rewrite the long exact sequence in cohomology givent by the short exact sequence $0\to C^{\bullet}[-1]\to [B^{\bullet}\to C^{\bullet-1}]\to B^{\bullet} \to 0$ wich is (as in the previous lemma): \[\ldots\to H^{k-1} B^{\bullet} \to H^{k-1} C^{\bullet}\to H^k[B^{\bullet}\to C^{\bullet-1}]\to H^k B^{\bullet}\to H^kC^{\bullet}\to \ldots\]. The result is then a long exact sequence : \[\ldots\to H^{k-1} B^{\bullet} \to H^{k-1} C^{\bullet}\to H^kA^{\bullet}\to H^k B^{\bullet}\to H^k C^{\bullet}\to\ldots\]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the three-term total complex as a cone, apply Lemma 1 to get a quasi-isomorphism, and substitute into the cone's long exact sequence.

nodes.name: Identify the three-term total complex with an iterated cone
nodes.statement: One can see that by construction there is a canonical isomorphism of complexess: $[A^{\bullet}\to B^{\bullet-1}\to C^{\bullet-2}]=[A^{\bullet}\to [B^{\bullet}\to C^{\bullet-1}]^{\bullet-1}]$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify the three-term total complex with an iterated cone.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 1: $A\to[B\to C]$ is a quasi-isomorphism
nodes.statement: Then by the previous lemma: $A^{\bullet}\to [B^{\bullet}\to C^{\bullet-1}]$ is a quasi isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 1: $A\to[B\to C]$ is a quasi-isomorphism.

nodes.name: Long exact sequence of the cone of $B\to C$
nodes.statement: One can then rewrite the long exact sequence in cohomology givent by the short exact sequence $0\to C^{\bullet}[-1]\to [B^{\bullet}\to C^{\bullet-1}]\to B^{\bullet} \to 0$ wich is (as in the previous lemma): \[\ldots\to  H^{k-1} B^{\bullet} \to H^{k-1} C^{\bullet}\to H^k[B^{\bullet}\to C^{\bullet-1}]\to H^k B^{\bullet}\to H^kC^{\bullet}\to \ldots\].
nodes.statement_short: Long exact sequence of the cone of $B\to C$.

nodes.name: Substitute to obtain the long exact sequence
nodes.statement: The result is then a long exact sequence : \[\ldots\to  H^{k-1} B^{\bullet} \to H^{k-1} C^{\bullet}\to H^kA^{\bullet}\to H^k B^{\bullet}\to H^k C^{\bullet}\to\ldots\]
nodes.statement_short: Substitute to obtain the long exact sequence.

nodes.name: Ambient space $X$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorf space.

nodes.name: Presheaf
nodes.statement: A presheave on $X$ is a contravariant functor from the category of open sets of $X$ to abélian groups.
differentia: from the category of open sets of $X$ to abélian groups
nodes.label: def:pre_sheaves

nodes.name: Stalk of a presheaf
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is a presheaf on $X$ and $p\in X$ then the stalk of $\mathcal{F}$ at $p$ is the abelian group $\mathcal{F}_p:=\varinjlim\limits_{p\in U\text{ open}}\mathcal{F}(U)$.
nodes.label: def:stalk

nodes.name: Sheaf
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is a presheaf on $X$, it is said to be a sheaf if for any $U\subset X$ open and any covering family of $U$ $(U_a)_{a\in A}$ one has the exact sequence: \begin{equation} 0\to \mathcal{F}(U)\to \prod\limits_{a\in A}\mathcal{F}(U_a)\to \prod\limits_{a,b\in A}\mathcal{F}(U_a\cap U_b) \end{equation}
differentia: for any $U\subset X$ open and any covering family of $U$ $(U_a)_{a\in A}$ one has the exact sequence
nodes.label: def:sheaves

nodes.name: Sheaf condition (Sh)
nodes.statement: 0\to \mathcal{F}(U)\to \prod\limits_{a\in A}\mathcal{F}(U_a)\to \prod\limits_{a,b\in A}\mathcal{F}(U_a\cap U_b)
nodes.label: axiom:Sh

nodes.name: $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf
nodes.statement: A $\mathcal{K}$-presheave on $X$ is a contravariant functor from the category of compact sets of $X$ to abélian groups.
differentia: from the category of compact sets of $X$ to abélian groups
nodes.label: def:K_pre_sheaves

nodes.name: Stalk of a $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is a $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf on $X$ and $p\in X$ then the stalk of $\mathcal{F}$ at $p$ is the abelian group $\mathcal{F}_p:=\varinjlim\limits_{p\in K\text{ compact}}\mathcal{F}(K)=\mathcal{F}(\{p\})$.
nodes.statement_short: Stalk of a $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf at $p$: colimit over compacts containing $p$, which equals $\mathcal{F}(\{p\})$.
nodes.label: def:K_stalk

nodes.name: $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is a $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf on $X$, it is said to be a $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf if the folowing conditions are satisfied:\begin{itemize} \item\begin{equation} \mathcal{F}(\varnothing)=0 \end{equation} \item For $K_1$ and $K_2$ two comapcts of $X$ the folowing sequence is exact:\begin{equation} 0\to\mathcal{F}(K_1\cup K_2)\to \mathcal{F}(K_1)\bigoplus\mathcal{F}(K_2)\to \mathcal{F}(K_1\cap K_2) \end{equation} \item For any compact $K$ of $X$, the following natural morphism is an isomorphism\begin{equation} \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U\text{ open relatively compact}}\mathcal{F}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{F}(K) \end{equation} \end{itemize}
differentia: For $K_1$ and $K_2$ two comapcts of $X$ the folowing sequence is exact
For any compact $K$ of $X$, the following natural morphism is an isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: A $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf vanishing on $\varnothing$, satisfying Mayer-Vietoris exactness for pairs of compacts, and continuity under shrinking relatively compact neighbourhoods.
nodes.label: def:K_sheaves

nodes.name: Axiom (Ksh1)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{F}(\varnothing)=0
nodes.label: axiom:Ksh1

nodes.name: Axiom (Ksh2)
nodes.statement: 0\to\mathcal{F}(K_1\cup K_2)\to \mathcal{F}(K_1)\bigoplus\mathcal{F}(K_2)\to \mathcal{F}(K_1\cap K_2)
nodes.label: axiom:Ksh2

nodes.name: Axiom (Ksh3)
nodes.statement: \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U\text{ open relatively compact}}\mathcal{F}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{F}(K)
nodes.label: axiom:Ksh3

nodes.name: Well-definedness of axiom (Ksh3)
nodes.statement: \eqref{axiom:Ksh3} is well defined because if $K$ is a compact subset of $X$, then for $x\in K$ let $U_x$ be an open neighborhood relatively compact (wich exists by local compactness), the family $(U_x)\ind{x}{K}$ covers $K$ then one can extract a finite cover of it : $U_1,\ldots U_n$ and then $\cup_{i=1}^n U_i$ is an open neighborhood, and a finite union of relatively comapct, then it's relatively compact. ($\overline{\cup_{i=1}^n U_i}=\cup_{i=1}^n \overline{U_i}$)
nodes.statement_short: Every compact has relatively compact open neighbourhoods (finite union of relatively compact opens), so the colimit in (Ksh3) is over a nonempty system.

nodes.name: Cofinal neighbourhoods of an intersection of compacts
nodes.statement: If $K_1,\ldots K_n$ are comapcts of $X$ then $\{U_1\cap\ldots\cap U_n\}_{U_i\supset K_i\text{ open in }X}$ is a cofinal system of neighborhoods of $K_1\cap \ldots \cap K_n$.
assumptions: $K_1,\ldots K_n$ are comapcts of $X$
conclusions: $\{U_1\cap\ldots\cap U_n\}_{U_i\supset K_i\text{ open in }X}$ is a cofinal system of neighborhoods of $K_1\cap \ldots \cap K_n$
nodes.label: lem:cofinal_syst_of_inter_compact

nodes.name: Adjunction with invertible unit and counit is an equivalence
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ are two categories, $F:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{D}$ and $G:\mathcal{D}\to \mathcal{C}$ two functors such that $(F,G)$ is an adjoint pair. Then for $(F,G)$ to be an equivalence of category, it's enough to have that thes canonical naturals transformations $\text{id}_{\mathcal{D}}\Rightarrow F\circ G$ and $G\circ F\Rightarrow \text{id}_{\mathcal{D}}$ are isomorphisms.

conclusions: for $(F,G)$ to be an equivalence of category, it's enough to have that thes canonical naturals transformations $\text{id}_{\mathcal{D}}\Rightarrow F\circ G$ and $G\circ F\Rightarrow \text{id}_{\mathcal{D}}$ are isomorphisms

nodes.name: Functors $\alpha^*$ and $\alpha_*$ between presheaves and $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item If $\mathcal{F}$ is a presheaf then let $\alpha^*\mathcal{F}$ be the $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf:\[K\mapsto \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open}}\mathcal{F}(U)\] \item If $\mathcal{G}$ is a $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf then let $\alpha_*\mathcal{G}$ be the presheaf:\[ U\mapsto \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K)\] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha^*\mathcal{F}(K)$ is the colimit of $\mathcal{F}(U)$ over opens $U\supset K$; $\alpha_*\mathcal{G}(U)$ is the limit of $\mathcal{G}(K)$ over compacts $K\subset U$.

nodes.statement: The pair $(\alpha^*,\alpha_*)$ is an adjonit pair.
conclusions: The pair $(\alpha^*,\alpha_*)$ is an adjonit pair.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a sheaf. The condition $\varnothing \subset U$ is always satisfied and $\varnothing$ is minimal among open subset for the inclusion then $(\alpha^*)(\mathcal{F})(\varnothing)=\mathcal{F}(\varnothing)$. One can apply the sheaf condition to the empty family and obtain the exact sequence $0\to \mathcal{F}(\varnothing)\to \Pi_{\varnothing}=0$, and then \eqref{axiom:Ksh1}.\\ Let $K_1,K_2$ be two of compacts of $X$, let $U_1,U_2$ be a two opens such that $K_i\subset U_i$ for all $i$. Then the sheaf condition gives an exact sequence (because for abelian groups the product is the direct sum) $0\to \mathcal{F}(U_1\cup U_2)\to \mathcal{F}(U_1)\bigoplus\mathcal{F}(U_2)\to \mathcal{F}(U_1\cap U_2)$. nodes.name: Show $\alpha^*\mathcal{F}$ satisfies (Ksh1)-(Ksh3)
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a sheaf. The condition $\varnothing \subset U$ is always satisfied and $\varnothing$ is minimal among open subset for the inclusion then $(\alpha^*)(\mathcal{F})(\varnothing)=\mathcal{F}(\varnothing)$. One can apply the sheaf condition to the empty family and obtain the exact sequence $0\to \mathcal{F}(\varnothing)\to \Pi_{\varnothing}=0$, and then \eqref{axiom:Ksh1}.\\

        Let $K_1,K_2$ be two of compacts of $X$, let $U_1,U_2$ be a two opens such that $K_i\subset U_i$ for all $i$. Then the sheaf condition gives an exact sequence (because for abelian groups the product is the direct sum) $0\to \mathcal{F}(U_1\cup U_2)\to \mathcal{F}(U_1)\bigoplus\mathcal{F}(U_2)\to \mathcal{F}(U_1\cap U_2)$. The injective limits are exacts then taking the limits over those opens gives an exact sequence: 
        \begin{equation} 0\to \varinjlim\limits_{K_i\subset U_i}\mathcal{F}(U_1\cup U_2)\to \varinjlim\limits_{K_i\subset U_i}\mathcal{F}(U_1)\times\mathcal{F}(U_2)\to \varinjlim\limits_{K_i\subset U_i}\mathcal{F}(U_1\cap U_2)
        \end{equation}

        An open $U$ contains $K_1\cup K_2$ if and only if it's of the form $U_1\cup U_2$ with $K_i\subset U_i$ (one can take $U_1=U_2=U$ for the direct implication), then by definition $\varinjlim\limits_{K_i\subset U_i}\mathcal{F}(U_1\cup U_2)=\alpha^*\mathcal{F}(K_1\cup K_2)$.\\
        
        The injective limit commute with the direct sum (as it is a coproduct), then: \[\varinjlim\limits_{K_i\subset U_i}\mathcal{F}(U_1)\times\mathcal{F}(U_2)=(\varinjlim\limits_{K_i\subset U_i}\mathcal{F}(U_1))\bigoplus(\varinjlim\limits_{K_i\subset U_i}\mathcal{F}(U_2))=\alpha^*\mathcal{F}(K_1)\bigoplus\alpha^*\mathcal{F}(K_2)\].\\
        
        By the lemma \ref{lem:cofinal_syst_of_inter_compact} the limit $\varinjlim\limits_{K_i\subset U_i}\mathcal{F}(U_1\cap U_2)$ compute the same thing as $\varinjlim\limits_{K_1\cap K_2\subset U}\mathcal{F}(U)=\alpha^*\mathcal{F}(K_1\cap K_2)$.\\

        Then the exact sequence \eqref{lim_of_sheaf_cond} is in fact \eqref{axiom:Ksh2}.\\ \\

        Let $K$ be a compact, $U$ a relatively comapct open such that $K\subset U$ and $V$ an open suche that $\overline{U}\subset V$ then $K\subset V$. Conversely if $V$ is an open containing $K$, then $K$ is a comapct of $V$ (locally compact as $X$ is) and then admits an open neighborhood $U$ relatively compact (in $V$).Thus (because the two limits are over the same set) one has the equality \[\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{open relatively compact}}\varinjlim\limits_{\overline{U}\subset V\text{ open}}\mathcal{F}(V)=\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U\ \text{open}}\mathcal{F}(V)\]. Wich rewrite by definition as $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U\ \text{open relatively compact}}\alpha^*\mathcal{F}(\overline{U})=\alpha^*\mathcal{F}(V)$ i.e. \eqref{axiom:Ksh3}.\\

        Then $\alpha^*\mathcal{F}$ is a $\Kc$-sheaf.

nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a $\Kc$-sheaf. Let $K_1,\ldots K_n$ be a family of compacts subsets let's show that the sequence $0\to \mathcal{G}(\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^n K_i)\to \prod\limits_{i=1}^n\mathcal{G}(K_i)\to \prod\limits_{i,j=1}^n\mathcal{G}(K_i\cap K_j)$.

Then by the exactness of \eqref{axiom:Ksh2} $f$ and $f_{n+1}$ are of the form $g|_K$ and $g|_{K_{n+1}}$, with $g\in \mathcal{G}(\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{n+1} K_i)$.
        
        Then $(f_1,\ldots,f_{n+1})$ is of the form $(g|_{K_1},\ldots g|_{K_{n+1}})$. Wicch conclude the exactness prof because the inclusion of the image into the kernel is starightforward by definition of the map.

        Let $(U_a)\ind{a}{A}$ be a family of opens of $X$, one can consider the collections of family of compacts $(K_a)\ind{a}{A}$  such that $\forall a\in A /\ K_a\subset U_a$ and only  a finite number of them are not empty (by the \eqref{axiom:Ksh1}adding enpty compacts in the family ad a product with zero in the exact sequence, wich does not changes the sequence) and take the projective limit of the previous exact sequence over it.

        The sequence remains exact because projective limits are left exacts: \[0\to\varprojlim\mathcal{G}(\bigcup\limits_{a\in A}K_a)\to \varprojlim\prod\limits_{a\in A}\mathcal{G}(K_a)\to \varprojlim\prod\limits_{a,b\in A}\mathcal{G}(K_a\cap K_b)\]. The projective limits commmute with products, then the sequence is 

        \[0\to\varprojlim\mathcal{G}(\bigcup\limits_{a\in A}K_a)\to \prod\limits_{a\in A}\varprojlim\mathcal{G}(K_a)\to\prod\limits_{a,b\in A}\varprojlim\mathcal{G}(K_a\cap K_b)\]

        By definition (because it's for a fixed $a$ and does not depend of the family for other indexes) $\varprojlim\mathcal{G}(K_a)=\alpha_*\mathcal{G}(U_a)$ and $\varprojlim\mathcal{G}(K_a\cap K_b)=\alpha_*\mathcal{G}(U_a\cap U_b)$. Any compact included in $\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a$ is included in a finite number of the opens then $\varprojlim\mathcal{G}(\bigcup\limits_{a\in A}K_a)$ compute $\alpha_*\mathcal{G}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)$, then one get's the sheaf condition for $\alpha_*\mathcal{G}$.

        Then $(f_1,\ldots,f_{n+1})$ is of the form $(g|_{K_1},\ldots g|_{K_{n+1}})$. Wicch conclude the exactness prof because the inclusion of the image into the kernel is starightforward by definition of the map.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: By using \ref{lem:equiv_of_adj}, it's enough to show that for any sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ and $\Kc$-sheaf $\mathcal{G}$, the natural maps $\mathcal{F}\to \alpha_*\alpha^*\mathcal{U}$ and $\alpha^*\alpha_*\mathcal{G}\to \mathcal{G}$ are isomorphism. The fact of being a natural isomorphism can be checked locally.\begin{itemize} \item Let $K$ be a comapct of $X$. One has to check that $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open}}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ is an isomorphism.\\ Let $U$ be an open relatively compact that contain $K$, for any $K'\subset U$ comapct,$\mathcal{G}$ define compatible maps $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K')$, then by the universal proprety of the projective limit one get's a map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ such that the map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ is $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K)$. Then by taking the inductive limit over $U$, one get's ($\mathcal{G}(K)$ does not depend on $U$) that the canonical morphism $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ factors that way: $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$. Then by $\eqref{axiom:Ksh3}$ it's enough to show that the map \[\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{open relatively compact}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{open relatively compact}}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\] is an isomorphism.\\ Let's build the map in the other direcction. By using the universal property of the inductive limit, one needs for any open relatively comapct $U$ that contains $K$ to build maps (compatibles with inclusion of opens) \[\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open relatively comapct}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\] $K$ is a compact of $U$, then let $V$ be an open subset (of $U$ then of $X$) such that $\overline{V}\subset U$. $\overline{V}$ is a compact in $U$ then there is a canonical projection $\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{V})$ and $V$ is an open relatively comapct that contains $K$ then there is a canonical inclusion $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open relatively comapct}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$, the composition of the two maps gives the desired morphism.\\ One has to chack that it does not depend of the choice of $V$. If $V'$ is an other choice, then $V\cup V'$ is an open subset of $U$ that contains $K$ and $\overline{V\cup V'}=\overline{V}\cup\overline{V'}\subset U$. $V\cap V'$ is an open subset of $U$ that contains $K$ and $\overline{V\cap V'}\subset \overline{V}\cap\overline{V'}\subset U$, then all the triangle of the following diagram are commutative (and thus the two morphism are equal): \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd} && {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V'})} \\ {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V\cup V'})} && {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V\cap V'})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\ && {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} \arrow[from=1-3, to=2-4] \arrow[from=1-3, to=2-5] \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3] \arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2] \arrow[from=2-1, to=3-3] \arrow[from=2-2, to=1-3] \arrow[from=2-2, to=3-3] \arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5] \arrow[from=3-3, to=2-4] \arrow[from=3-3, to=2-5] \end{tikzcd}\end{center} If $W$ is an open relatively compact that contains $U$ then (by universal property of the projective limit) there is a commutative triangle : \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd} {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} \\ {\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3] \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-1] \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3] \end{tikzcd}\end{center} Then the triangle is also commutative: \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd} {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\ {\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3] \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-1] \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3] \end{tikzcd}\end{center} That concludes the compatibility condition.\\ Let's now check that the two maps are the inverse of one another. If $U$ and $V$ are opens relatively compacts of $X$ such that $K\subset V\subset U$, and $W$ is an open such that $K\subset W\subset \overline{W}\subset V$, then y the previous constructions, the following diagram is commutative: \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd} {\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} && {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\ & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\ {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} && {\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3] \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2] \arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1] \arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3] \arrow[from=1-3, to=2-4] \arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3] \arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4] \arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5] \arrow[from=3-1, to=2-2] \arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3] \arrow[from=3-3, to=2-3] \arrow[from=3-3, to=2-4] \end{tikzcd}\end{center} In particular to conclude that the following square is commutative: \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd} {\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\ \\ {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3] \arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1] \arrow[from=1-3, to=3-3] \arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3] \end{tikzcd}\end{center} One has to check that the morphism $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$ is the canonical inclusion. By the compatibility condition of the universal property of the projective limit $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})$ is the map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V}\supset \overline{W})$. And the maps $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$ is the canonical inclusion by the compatibility condition of the universal property of the injective limit. However by the universal property of the inductive limit the only morphism that make this diagram commute is the identity.\\ For the other direction, one keeps the same notations. By the previous constructions the following diagram is commutative: \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd} {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\ {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} &&& {\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\ &&& {\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\ {\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1] \arrow[from=1-1, to=2-4] \arrow[from=2-1, to=2-4] \arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5] \arrow[from=2-4, to=3-4] \arrow[from=2-5, to=3-5] \arrow[from=3-4, to=3-5] \arrow[from=4-1, to=2-1] \arrow[from=4-1, to=2-4] \end{tikzcd}\end{center} One can remark that the map $\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ is the canonical map. By the universal property of the projective limit, it's enough to show that it's true when postcomposed by the maps (for K' a compact of $W$)$\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to\mathcal{G}(K')$. By construction $\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to\mathcal{G}(K')=\mathcal{G}(\overline{W}\subset K')$, so the statment is a compatibility condition in the universal property of the projective limit. Then by the compatibility condition of the universal property of the inductive limit the map $\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ is also the canonical map. Then the following diagram is commutative: \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd} {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\ \\ {\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3] \arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1] \arrow[from=1-3, to=3-3] \arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3] \end{tikzcd}\end{center} An again by uniqueness it must be the identity, that concludes the proof. \item Let $U$ be an open of $X$. One has to check that $\mathcal{F}(U)\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K \text{ compact}}\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U' \text{ open}}\mathcal{F}(U')$ is an isomorphism. One can apply the previous item with the compact $K=\{p\}$ (for $p\in X$) and then get that $\alpha_*$ preserve the stlaks. The fact that $\alpha^*$ preserves the stalks is straightforward by definition. Then the map $\mathcal{F}(U)\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K \text{ compact}}\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U' \text{ open}}\mathcal{F}(U')$ is an isomorphism once restricted to stalks, and because the two are sheaves on $X$ they are then isomorphics. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Counit $\alpha^*\alpha_*\mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{G}$ is an isomorphism
nodes.statement:
Let $K$ be a comapct of $X$. One has to check that $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open}}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ is an isomorphism.\\

        Let $U$ be an open relatively compact that contain $K$, for any $K'\subset U$ comapct,$\mathcal{G}$ define compatible maps $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K')$, then by the universal proprety of the projective limit one get's a map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ such that the map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ is $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K)$. Then by taking the inductive limit over $U$, one get's ($\mathcal{G}(K)$ does not depend on $U$) that the canonical morphism $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ factors that way: $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$. Then by $\eqref{axiom:Ksh3}$ it's enough to show that the map \[\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{open relatively compact}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{open relatively compact}}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\] is an isomorphism.\\
        
        Let's build the map in the other direcction. By using the universal property of the inductive limit, one needs for any open relatively comapct $U$ that contains $K$ to build maps (compatibles with inclusion of opens) \[\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open relatively comapct}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\]

        $K$ is a compact of $U$, then let $V$ be an open subset (of $U$ then of $X$) such that $\overline{V}\subset U$. $\overline{V}$ is a compact in $U$ then there is a canonical projection $\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{V})$ and $V$ is an open relatively comapct that contains $K$ then there is a canonical inclusion $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open relatively comapct}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$, the composition of the two maps gives the desired morphism.\\

        One has to chack that it does not depend of the choice of $V$. If $V'$ is an other choice, then $V\cup V'$ is an open subset of $U$ that contains $K$ and $\overline{V\cup V'}=\overline{V}\cup\overline{V'}\subset U$. $V\cap V'$ is an open subset of $U$ that contains $K$ and $\overline{V\cap V'}\subset \overline{V}\cap\overline{V'}\subset U$, then all the triangle of the following diagram are commutative (and thus the two morphism are equal):

        
\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	&& {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V'})} \\
	{\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V\cup V'})} && {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V\cap V'})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
	&& {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})}
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}

    If $W$ is an open relatively compact that contains $U$ then (by universal property of the projective limit) there is a commutative triangle :

    
\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} \\
	{\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}
    Then the triangle is also commutative:
    \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
        {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
        {\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
        \arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
        \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-1]
        \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3]
    \end{tikzcd}\end{center}

    That concludes the compatibility condition.\\

    Let's now check that the two maps are the inverse of one another. If $U$ and $V$ are opens relatively compacts of $X$ such that $K\subset V\subset U$, and $W$ is an open such that $K\subset W\subset \overline{W}\subset V$, then y the previous constructions, the following diagram is commutative:
    
\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} && {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\
	& {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
	{\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} && {\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-4]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}

In particular to conclude that the following square is commutative:


\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
	\\
	{\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}
    One has to check that the morphism $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$ is the canonical inclusion. By the compatibility condition of the universal property of the projective limit $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})$ is the map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V}\supset \overline{W})$. And the maps $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$ is the canonical inclusion by the compatibility condition of the universal property of the injective limit.

    However by the universal property of the inductive limit the only morphism that make this diagram commute is the identity.\\

    For the other direction, one keeps the same notations. By the previous constructions the following diagram is commutative:
    
\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\
	{\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} &&& {\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
	&&& {\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\
	{\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=3-4]
	\arrow[from=2-5, to=3-5]
	\arrow[from=3-4, to=3-5]
	\arrow[from=4-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=4-1, to=2-4]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}

    One can remark that the map $\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ is the canonical map. By the universal property of the projective limit, it's enough to show that it's true when postcomposed by the maps (for K' a compact of $W$)$\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to\mathcal{G}(K')$. By construction $\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to\mathcal{G}(K')=\mathcal{G}(\overline{W}\subset K')$, so the statment is a compatibility condition in the universal property of the projective limit.

    Then by the compatibility condition of the universal property of the inductive limit the map $\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ is also the canonical map. Then the following diagram is commutative: 
    
    \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\
	\\
	{\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
    \end{tikzcd}\end{center}

    An again by uniqueness it must be the identity, that concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Counit $\alpha^*\alpha_*\mathcal{G}\to\mathcal{G}$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: State the counit at a compact $K$
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a comapct of $X$. One has to check that $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open}}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: State the counit at a compact $K$.

nodes.name: Factor the (Ksh3) map; reduce to a comparison of colimits
nodes.statement: Let $U$ be an open relatively compact that contain $K$, for any $K'\subset U$ comapct,$\mathcal{G}$ define compatible maps $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K')$, then by the universal proprety of the projective limit one get's a map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ such that the map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ is $\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K)$. Then by taking the inductive limit over $U$, one get's ($\mathcal{G}(K)$ does not depend on $U$) that the canonical morphism $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{G}(K)$ factors that way: $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(K)$. Then by $\eqref{axiom:Ksh3}$ it's enough to show that the map \[\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{open relatively compact}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{open relatively compact}}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\] is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Factor the (Ksh3) map; reduce to a comparison of colimits.

nodes.name: Construct the inverse map via a smaller neighbourhood $V$
nodes.statement:
Let's build the map in the other direcction. By using the universal property of the inductive limit, one needs for any open relatively comapct $U$ that contains $K$ to build maps (compatibles with inclusion of opens) \[\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open relatively comapct}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})\]

        $K$ is a compact of $U$, then let $V$ be an open subset (of $U$ then of $X$) such that $\overline{V}\subset U$. $\overline{V}$ is a compact in $U$ then there is a canonical projection $\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K' \text{ compact}}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{V})$ and $V$ is an open relatively comapct that contains $K$ then there is a canonical inclusion $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open relatively comapct}}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$, the composition of the two maps gives the desired morphism.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the inverse map via a smaller neighbourhood $V$.

nodes.name: Independence of $V$ and compatibility with inclusions
nodes.statement:
One has to chack that it does not depend of the choice of $V$. If $V'$ is an other choice, then $V\cup V'$ is an open subset of $U$ that contains $K$ and $\overline{V\cup V'}=\overline{V}\cup\overline{V'}\subset U$. $V\cap V'$ is an open subset of $U$ that contains $K$ and $\overline{V\cap V'}\subset \overline{V}\cap\overline{V'}\subset U$, then all the triangle of the following diagram are commutative (and thus the two morphism are equal):

        
\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	&& {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V'})} \\
	{\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V\cup V'})} && {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V\cap V'})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
	&& {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})}
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}

    If $W$ is an open relatively compact that contains $U$ then (by universal property of the projective limit) there is a commutative triangle :

    
\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} \\
	{\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}
    Then the triangle is also commutative:
    \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
        {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
        {\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
        \arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
        \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-1]
        \arrow[from=2-1, to=1-3]
    \end{tikzcd}\end{center}

    That concludes the compatibility condition.
nodes.statement_short: Independence of $V$ and compatibility with inclusions.

nodes.name: One composite is the identity by universal property of colimits
nodes.statement:
Let's now check that the two maps are the inverse of one another. If $U$ and $V$ are opens relatively compacts of $X$ such that $K\subset V\subset U$, and $W$ is an open such that $K\subset W\subset \overline{W}\subset V$, then y the previous constructions, the following diagram is commutative:
    
\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} && {\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\
	& {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
	{\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} && {\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=2-4]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}

In particular to conclude that the following square is commutative:


\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
	\\
	{\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}
    One has to check that the morphism $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$ is the canonical inclusion. By the compatibility condition of the universal property of the projective limit $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})$ is the map $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V}\supset \overline{W})$. And the maps $\mathcal{G}(\overline{V})\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})$ is the canonical inclusion by the compatibility condition of the universal property of the injective limit.

    However by the universal property of the inductive limit the only morphism that make this diagram commute is the identity.
nodes.statement_short: One composite is the identity by universal property of colimits.

nodes.name: Other composite is the identity by uniqueness
nodes.statement:
For the other direction, one keeps the same notations. By the previous constructions the following diagram is commutative:
    
\begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\
	{\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} &&& {\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\mathcal{G}(\overline{U})} \\
	&&& {\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} & {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\
	{\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=3-4]
	\arrow[from=2-5, to=3-5]
	\arrow[from=3-4, to=3-5]
	\arrow[from=4-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=4-1, to=2-4]
\end{tikzcd}\end{center}

    One can remark that the map $\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ is the canonical map. By the universal property of the projective limit, it's enough to show that it's true when postcomposed by the maps (for K' a compact of $W$)$\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to\mathcal{G}(K')$. By construction $\mathcal{G}(\overline{W})\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to\mathcal{G}(K')=\mathcal{G}(\overline{W}\subset K')$, so the statment is a compatibility condition in the universal property of the projective limit.

    Then by the compatibility condition of the universal property of the inductive limit the map $\varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varprojlim\limits_{W\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')\to \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')$ is also the canonical map. Then the following diagram is commutative: 
    
    \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd}
	{\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} \\
	\\
	{\varprojlim\limits_{V\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')} && {\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U}\varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K'}\mathcal{G}(K')}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
    \end{tikzcd}\end{center}

    An again by uniqueness it must be the identity, that concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Other composite is the identity by uniqueness.

nodes.name: Unit is an isomorphism: both preserve stalks
nodes.statement:
Let $U$ be an open of $X$. One has to check that $\mathcal{F}(U)\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K \text{ compact}}\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U' \text{ open}}\mathcal{F}(U')$ is an isomorphism.

        One can apply the previous item with the compact $K=\{p\}$ (for $p\in X$) and then get that $\alpha_*$ preserve the stlaks. The fact that $\alpha^*$ preserves the stalks is straightforward by definition. Then the map $\mathcal{F}(U)\to \varprojlim\limits_{U\supset K \text{ compact}}\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U' \text{ open}}\mathcal{F}(U')$ is an isomorphism once restricted to stalks, and because the two are sheaves on $X$ they are then isomorphics.
nodes.statement_short: Unit is an isomorphism: both preserve stalks.

nodes.name: Cohomology $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf of a complex
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves then taking the cohomology defines a $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf denoted $H^{\bullet}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$.
nodes.label: def:cohomology_of_k-prsh

nodes.name: Quasi-isomorphism of complexes of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves
nodes.statement: A morphisme of complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheave $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ is called quasi-isomorphism if it induces isomorphisms $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to H^i\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ for all $i$.
differentia: it induces isomorphisms $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to H^i\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ for all $i$
nodes.label: def:quasi_iso_of_complex_of_k-prsh

nodes.name: Homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf
nodes.statement: A complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ is said to be a Homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheave if the folowing conditions are satisfied:\begin{itemize} \item\begin{equation} \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(\varnothing) \text{ is an acyclic complex} \end{equation} \item For $K_1$ and $K_2$ two comapcts of $X$ the folowing complex is acyclic:\begin{equation} [\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1\cup K_2)\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet-1}(K_1)\bigoplus\mathcal{F}^{\bullet-1}(K_2)\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet-2}(K_1\cap K_2) ] \end{equation} \item For any compact $K$ of $X$, the following natural morphism is a quasi-isomorphism \begin{equation} \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U\text{ open relatively compact}}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K) \end{equation} \end{itemize}
differentia: For $K_1$ and $K_2$ two comapcts of $X$ the folowing complex is acyclic
For any compact $K$ of $X$, the following natural morphism is a quasi-isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Derived analogue of a $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf: acyclic on $\varnothing$, acyclic Mayer-Vietoris total complex, and (Ksh3) up to quasi-isomorphism.
nodes.label: def:homotopy_k_sheaf

nodes.name: Axiom (hKsh1)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(\varnothing) \text{ is an acyclic complex}
nodes.label: axiom:hKsh1

nodes.name: Axiom (hKsh2)
nodes.statement: [\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1\cup K_2)\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet-1}(K_1)\bigoplus\mathcal{F}^{\bullet-1}(K_2)\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet-2}(K_1\cap K_2) ]
nodes.label: axiom:hKsh2

nodes.name: Axiom (hKsh3)
nodes.statement: \varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U\text{ open relatively compact}}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(\overline{U})\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K)
nodes.label: axiom:hKsh3

nodes.name: Mayer-Vietoris long exact sequence
nodes.statement: By using \ref{lem:complex_total_of_three_is_acyclic}, \eqref{axiom:hKsh3} give rise to a "Mayer-Vietoris" long exact sequence: \[\ldots \to H^k \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1\cup K_2)\to H^k \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1)\bigoplus H^k\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_2)\to H^k \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1\cap K_2)\to \ldots\]
conclusions: give rise to a "Mayer-Vietoris" long exact sequence: \[\ldots \to H^k \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1\cup K_2)\to H^k \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1)\bigoplus H^k\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_2)\to H^k \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1\cap K_2)\to \ldots\]
nodes.label: lem:Mayer_Vietoris

nodes.name: Homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaves are stable under extension
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves. If $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ has a finite filtration whose associated graded is a Homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf, then $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ is a Homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves.
$\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ has a finite filtration whose associated graded is a Homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf
nodes.label: lem:homotpy_k_sheaves_stable_by_extension

nodes.name: First nonzero cohomology of a homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf is a $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ is a homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf, and $H^{-1}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}=0$ then $H^{0}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ is a $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf
assumptions: $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ is a homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf
$H^{-1}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}=0$
nodes.label: lem:first_non_zero_homology_of_homotopy_k_sheaf_is_k_sheaf

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(\varnothing)$ is acyclic then in particular it's cohomology in degre $0$ is $0$, then one gets \eqref{axiom:Ksh1} \item $H^{-1}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1\cap K_2)=0$ then the first terms \ref{lem:Mayer_Vietoris} gives the exact sequence of \eqref{axiom:Ksh2} \item Let $K$ be a compact of $X$, the quasi-isomorphism of \eqref{axiom:Ksh3} gives (in particular) that $H^0\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K)=H^0(\varinjlim\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(\bar{U}))$. To conclude one has to apply that the cohomology commute with inductive limit of a complex (Bouraki algèbre prop 1 X.28) and that in the category of presheaves of abélian groups, the limits are computed objectvise. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Check (Ksh1)-(Ksh3) for $H^0$: acyclicity on $\varnothing$, the start of the Mayer-Vietoris sequence, and cohomology commuting with filtered colimits.

nodes.name: (Ksh1) from acyclicity on $\varnothing$
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(\varnothing)$ is acyclic then in particular it's cohomology in degre $0$ is $0$, then one gets \eqref{axiom:Ksh1}
nodes.statement_short: (Ksh1) from acyclicity on $\varnothing$.

nodes.name: (Ksh2) from the beginning of the Mayer-Vietoris sequence
nodes.statement: $H^{-1}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K_1\cap K_2)=0$ then the first terms \ref{lem:Mayer_Vietoris} gives the exact sequence of \eqref{axiom:Ksh2}
nodes.statement_short: (Ksh2) from the beginning of the Mayer-Vietoris sequence.

nodes.name: (Ksh3) since cohomology commutes with filtered colimits (Bourbaki)
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a compact of $X$, the quasi-isomorphism of \eqref{axiom:Ksh3} gives (in particular) that $H^0\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K)=H^0(\varinjlim\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(\bar{U}))$. To conclude one has to apply that the cohomology commute with inductive limit of a complex (Bouraki algèbre prop 1 X.28) and that in the category of presheaves of abélian groups, the limits are computed objectvise.
nodes.statement_short: (Ksh3) since cohomology commutes with filtered colimits (Bourbaki).

nodes.name: Spaces $X$, $Y$ and continuous map $f$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two loccaly compacts hausdorf spaces and $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map.

nodes.name: Pushforward of a presheaf
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is a pre-sheaf over $X$, then the rule $U\mapsto \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U))$ defines a pre-shaef over $Y$. The functor obtained is denoted $f_*$ and named the pushforward by $f$. $f_*$ send sheaves over $X$ into sheaves over $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: $f_*\mathcal{F}(U)=\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U))$, the pushforward; it preserves sheaves.
nodes.label: def:pushforward_of_sheaf

nodes.name: Pushforward preserves sheaves
nodes.statement: $f_*$ send sheaves over $X$ into sheaves over $Y$.
conclusions: $f_*$ send sheaves over $X$ into sheaves over $Y$.

nodes.name: Proof that pushforward preserves sheaves
nodes.statement: Let $(U_a)\ind{a}{A}$ be a family of opens of $Y$. Then one ca apply the sheaf condition of $\mathcal{F}$ with the family of opens of $X$: $(f^{-1}(U_a))\ind{a}{A}$. The result is the exact sequence: \[0\to \mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}f^{-1}(U_a))\to \prod\limits_{a\in A}\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U_a))\to \prod\limits_{a,b\in A}\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U_a)\cap f^{-1}(U_b))\]. On the other hand, the inverse image commute with union and intersections, then the previous exact sequence rewrites to \[0\to f_*\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)\to \prod\limits_{a\in A}f_*\mathcal{F}(U_a)\to \prod\limits_{a,b\in A}f_*\mathcal{F}(U_a\cap U_b)\]. In other words, $f_*\mathcal{F}$ is a sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the sheaf condition of $\mathcal{F}$ to the preimage cover; preimages commute with unions and intersections.

nodes.name: Take a cover of $Y$ and apply the sheaf condition to its preimage
nodes.statement: Let $(U_a)\ind{a}{A}$ be a family of opens of $Y$. Then one ca apply the sheaf condition of $\mathcal{F}$ with the family of opens of $X$: $(f^{-1}(U_a))\ind{a}{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a cover of $Y$ and apply the sheaf condition to its preimage.

nodes.name: Resulting exact sequence for $\mathcal{F}$
nodes.statement: The result is the exact sequence: \[0\to \mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}f^{-1}(U_a))\to \prod\limits_{a\in A}\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U_a))\to \prod\limits_{a,b\in A}\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U_a)\cap f^{-1}(U_b))\].
nodes.statement_short: Resulting exact sequence for $\mathcal{F}$.

nodes.name: Rewrite via preimages commuting with unions and intersections
nodes.statement: On the other hand, the inverse image commute with union and intersections, then the previous exact sequence rewrites to \[0\to f_*\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)\to \prod\limits_{a\in A}f_*\mathcal{F}(U_a)\to \prod\limits_{a,b\in A}f_*\mathcal{F}(U_a\cap U_b)\].
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite via preimages commuting with unions and intersections.

nodes.name: Conclude $f_*\mathcal{F}$ is a sheaf
nodes.statement: In other words, $f_*\mathcal{F}$ is a sheaf.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $f_*\mathcal{F}$ is a sheaf.

nodes.name: Pullback of a sheaf
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is a pre-sheaf over $Y$, then the rule $U\mapsto \varinjlim\limits_{f(U)\subset V}\mathcal{F}(V)$ defines a pre-sheaf over $Y$. If $\mathcal{F}$ is a sheaf, the sheafification of the previous pre-sheaf is a denoted $f^*\mathcal{F}$ and called the pullback by $f$.
nodes.statement_short: $f^*\mathcal{F}$ is the sheafification of $U\mapsto\varinjlim_{f(U)\subset V}\mathcal{F}(V)$.
nodes.label: def:pullback_of_sheaf

nodes.name: Exceptional pushforward along an open inclusion
nodes.statement: If $f:X\to Y$ is the inclusion of an open subset, the exceptional pushforward by $f$: $f_!$ is defined by $f_!\mathcal{F}(U)$ being the subset of $f_*\mathcal{F}(U)$ of sections that vanish over a neighborhood of $Y-X$. It send the sheaves over $X$ into the sheaves over $Y$
nodes.statement_short: For an open inclusion, $f_!\mathcal{F}(U)$ consists of sections of $f_*\mathcal{F}(U)$ vanishing near $Y-X$; it preserves sheaves.
nodes.label: def:exceptional_pushforward_of_sheaf

nodes.name: Exceptional pushforward preserves sheaves
nodes.statement: It send the sheaves over $X$ into the sheaves over $Y$
conclusions: It send the sheaves over $X$ into the sheaves over $Y$

nodes.name: Proof that exceptional pushforward preserves sheaves
nodes.statement: Let $U\supset V$ be two opens of $Y$ and $h$ be an element of $f_!\mathcal{F}(U)$, then $h$ is an element of $\mathcal{F}(U\cap X)$ such that there is a $W$ open that contains $Y\backslash X$ and such that $h|_{U\cap W\cap X}=0$. Then $0=h|_V|_{U\cap W\cap X}=h|_{V\cap U\cap W\cap X}=h|_{V\cap W\cap X}$ so $h|_V$ is in $f_!\mathcal{F}(V)$. So $f_!\mathcal{F}$ is well defined. Let $(U_a)\ind{a}{A}$ be a family of opens of $Y$. The map $f_!\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a\cap X)\to\prod\limits\ind{a}{A}f_!\mathcal{F}(U_a)$ is a reistriction of an injective map (because of the sheaf condition of $f_*\mathcal{F}$), then it's also injective. Let $(h_a)$ be an element of the kernel of $\prod\limits_{a\in A}f_!\mathcal{F}(U_a)\to \prod\limits_{a,b\in A}f_!\mathcal{F}(U_a\cap U_b)$. By the sheaf condition of $f_*\mathcal{F}$, it's of the form $(h|_{U_a})$ with $h\in f_*\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)$. To conclude the sheaf condition for $f_!\mathcal{F}$ one has to check that $h$ is $f_!\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)$. By definition for any $a\in A$ there is an open $V_a$ of $Y$ that contains $Y\backslash X$ and such that $h_a|_{U_a\cap V_a\cap X}=0$. So for all $a\in A\, h_{U_a\cap V_a\cap X}=0$. Let $V$ be the union of the $V_a$, it contains $Y\backslash X$. the reistriction of $h|_V$ to all $V_a\cap X$ are $0$, then by the first part of the sheaf condition, $h|_{V\cap X}$ is also $0$, then $h$ is in $f_!\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Check restriction preserves vanishing near $Y\setminus X$, then inherit injectivity and gluing from $f_*\mathcal{F}$ and show the glued section vanishes near $Y\setminus X$.

nodes.name: $f_!\mathcal{F}$ is a presheaf
nodes.statement: Let $U\supset V$ be two opens of $Y$ and $h$ be an element of $f_!\mathcal{F}(U)$, then $h$ is an element of $\mathcal{F}(U\cap X)$ such that there is a $W$ open that contains $Y\backslash X$ and such that $h|_{U\cap W\cap X}=0$. Then  $0=h|_V|_{U\cap W\cap X}=h|_{V\cap U\cap W\cap X}=h|_{V\cap W\cap X}$ so $h|_V$ is in $f_!\mathcal{F}(V)$. So $f_!\mathcal{F}$ is well defined.
nodes.statement_short: $f_!\mathcal{F}$ is a presheaf.

nodes.name: Injectivity from the sheaf condition of $f_*\mathcal{F}$
nodes.statement: Let $(U_a)\ind{a}{A}$ be a family of opens of $Y$. The map $f_!\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a\cap X)\to\prod\limits\ind{a}{A}f_!\mathcal{F}(U_a)$ is a reistriction of an injective map (because of the sheaf condition of $f_*\mathcal{F}$), then it's also injective.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity from the sheaf condition of $f_*\mathcal{F}$.

nodes.name: Glue in $f_*\mathcal{F}$; reduce to support condition
nodes.statement: Let $(h_a)$ be an element of the kernel of $\prod\limits_{a\in A}f_!\mathcal{F}(U_a)\to \prod\limits_{a,b\in A}f_!\mathcal{F}(U_a\cap U_b)$. By the sheaf condition of $f_*\mathcal{F}$, it's of the form $(h|_{U_a})$ with $h\in f_*\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)$. To conclude the sheaf condition for $f_!\mathcal{F}$ one has to check that $h$ is $f_!\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue in $f_*\mathcal{F}$; reduce to support condition.

nodes.name: Glued section vanishes near $Y\setminus X$
nodes.statement: By definition for any $a\in A$ there is an open $V_a$ of $Y$ that contains $Y\backslash X$ and such that $h_a|_{U_a\cap V_a\cap X}=0$. So for all $a\in A\, h_{U_a\cap V_a\cap X}=0$. Let $V$ be the union of the $V_a$, it contains $Y\backslash X$. the reistriction of $h|_V$ to all $V_a\cap X$ are $0$, then by the first part of the sheaf condition, $h|_{V\cap X}$ is also $0$, then $h$ is in $f_!\mathcal{F}(\bigcup\limits\ind{a}{A}U_a)$.
nodes.statement_short: Glued section vanishes near $Y\setminus X$.

nodes.name: $f$ is proper
nodes.statement: Let's assume that $f$ is proper.

nodes.name: Preimages of neighbourhoods form a basis around $f^{-1}(K)$
nodes.statement: If $K$ is a compact of $Y$, then $\{f^{-1}(U)\}_{K\subset U}$ is a basis of open neighborhoods of $f^{-1}(K)$.
assumptions: $K$ is a compact of $Y$
conclusions: $\{f^{-1}(U)\}_{K\subset U}$ is a basis of open neighborhoods of $f^{-1}(K)$
nodes.label: lem:basis_of_open_of_fm1K

nodes.name: Pushforward of a $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}$ is a pre-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf over $X$, then the rule $K\mapsto \mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(K))$ defines a pre-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf over $Y$. The functor obtained is denoted $f_*$ and named the pushforward by $f$. $f_*$ send $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves over $X$ into $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves over $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: $f_*\mathcal{F}(K)=\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(K))$ for $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves; for proper $f$ it preserves $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves.
nodes.label: def:pushforward_of_K-sheaf

nodes.name: Pushforward preserves $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves
nodes.statement: $f_*$ send $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves over $X$ into $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves over $Y$.

nodes.name: Proof that pushforward preserves $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves
nodes.statement: By the lemma \ref{lem:basis_of_open_of_fm1K}, for $K$ a compact of $Y$, $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open in Y}}\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U))$ computes $\varinjlim\limits_{f^-1(K)\subset U \text{ open in X}}\mathcal{F}(U)$. In other words $f_*(\alpha^*\mathcal{F})=\alpha^*f_*(\mathcal{F})$. Then if $\mathcal{G}$ is a $\Kc$-sheaf, it's of the form $\alpha^*\mathcal{F}$ for $\mathcal{F}$ some sheaf. Then $f_*\mathcal{G}$ is isomorphic to $\alpha^*f_*(\mathcal{F})$ wich is a sheaf because of \ref{def:pushforward_of_sheaf} and \ref{lem:adj_kshv_and_shv}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 10 gives $f_*\alpha^*=\alpha^*f_*$; write a $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf as $\alpha^*\mathcal{F}$ and use that $f_*$ preserves sheaves.

nodes.name: Lemma 10: $f_*$ commutes with $\alpha^*$
nodes.statement: By the lemma \ref{lem:basis_of_open_of_fm1K}, for $K$ a compact of $Y$, $\varinjlim\limits_{K\subset U \text{ open in Y}}\mathcal{F}(f^{-1}(U))$ computes $\varinjlim\limits_{f^-1(K)\subset U \text{ open in X}}\mathcal{F}(U)$. In other words $f_*(\alpha^*\mathcal{F})=\alpha^*f_*(\mathcal{F})$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 10: $f_*$ commutes with $\alpha^*$.

nodes.name: Write $\mathcal{G}=\alpha^*\mathcal{F}$ and conclude
nodes.statement: Then if $\mathcal{G}$ is a $\Kc$-sheaf, it's of the form $\alpha^*\mathcal{F}$ for $\mathcal{F}$ some sheaf. Then $f_*\mathcal{G}$ is isomorphic to $\alpha^*f_*(\mathcal{F})$ wich is a sheaf because of \ref{def:pushforward_of_sheaf} and \ref{lem:adj_kshv_and_shv}
nodes.statement_short: Write $\mathcal{G}=\alpha^*\mathcal{F}$ and conclude.

nodes.name: Čech cohomology of a sheaf
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a topological space, and $\mathcal{F}$ a sheaf over $X$, then let $\check{H}^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F}))$ be the \v{C}ech cohomology of $X$ with coeficient in $\mathcal{F}$
nodes.label: def:chech_of_sh

nodes.name: Čech cohomology with support in a compact
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a topological space, $K$ a comapct subset of $X$ and $\mathcal{F}$ a sheaf over $X$, then let $\check{H}_K^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F}))$ be the \v{C}ech cohomology of $X$ with support in $K$ with coeficient in $\mathcal{F}$
nodes.label: def:chech_of_compact_sup_of_sh

nodes.name: Pullback maps in Čech cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map between topological spaces, and $\mathcal{F}$ a sheaf over $X$. $f$ induces a natural map $\check{H}^{\bullet}(Y;f_*\mathcal{F})\to \check{H}^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F})$.\\ Moreover if $f$ is proper, one gets a natural map $\check{H}_c^{\bullet}(Y;f_*\mathcal{F})\to \check{H}_c^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F})$
nodes.label: def:pullback_for_chech

nodes.name: Compactly supported Čech cohomology and exceptional pushforward
nodes.statement: Let $f:X\to Y$ be an inclusion of open subset, then there is a natural isomorphism $f_!:\check{H}_c^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F})\to \check{H}^{\bullet}(Y;f_!\mathcal{F})$
assumptions: $f:X\to Y$ be an inclusion of open subset
nodes.label: lem:chech_comm_with_exceptional

nodes.name: Čech cohomology of a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves on a compact space $X$ then we define the \v{C}ech cohomology $\check{H}(X;\mathcal{F}^{\bullet})$ by TODO
nodes.label: def:chech_of_compelx_of_k_prsh

nodes.name: Čech cohomology of a $\mathcal{K}$-presheaf
nodes.statement: By using the inclusion of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves into complexes of $\mathcal{K}$-presheave, one get's a definition of \v{C}ech cohomology for $\mathcal{K}$-presheave.
nodes.label: def:chech_of_k_prsh

nodes.name: Čech cohomology of an acyclic complex vanishes
nodes.statement: Let $mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be an acyclic complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves, then $\check{H}^k(X;mathcal{F}^{\bullet})=0$
assumptions: Let $mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be an acyclic complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves
nodes.label: lem:chech_of_acyclic_is_zero

nodes.name: Long exact sequence in Čech cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $0\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \mathcal{G}^{\bullet}\to \mathcal{H}^{\bullet}\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves. Then there is a long exact seuquence in \v{c}ech cohomology: \[\ldots\to \check{H}^k(X;\mathcal{F}^{\bullet})\to \check{H}^k(X;\mathcal{G}^{\bullet})\to \check{H}^k(X;\mathcal{H}^{\bullet})\to \ldots\]
assumptions: Let $0\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \mathcal{G}^{\bullet}\to \mathcal{H}^{\bullet}\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves.
conclusions: there is a long exact seuquence in \v{c}ech cohomology
nodes.label: lem:chech_long_exact_sequence

nodes.name: Čech cohomology preserves quasi-isomorphisms
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ is a quasi-isomorphism then the induced maps $\check{H}^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \check{H}^i\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ are isomorphims.
assumptions: $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ is a quasi-isomorphism
nodes.label: lem:chech_preserve_quasi_iso

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 14
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:q-iso_iff_cone_acyclic}, the complex $[\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \mathcal{G}^{\bullet-1}]$ is acyclic then by \ref{lem:chech_of_acyclic_is_zero}, it's \v{c}ech cohomology is zero. But there is a short exact sequence $0\to \mathcal{G}^{\bullet}[-1]\to [\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \mathcal{G}^{\bullet-1}]\to \mathcal{F}^{\bullet} \to 0$, then the long exact sequence induced by \ref{lem:chech_long_exact_sequence} gives the claimed isomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: The cone is acyclic (Lemma 1) so has zero Čech cohomology (Lemma 12); the Čech long exact sequence of the cone (Lemma 13) gives the isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Homotopy-$\mathcal{K}$-sheaf cohomology computes Čech cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves that verify \eqref{axiom:hKsh1} and \eqref{axiom:hKsh2} then the canonical map $H^{\bullet}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \check{H}^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F}^{\bullet})$ is an isomorphism.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves that verify \eqref{axiom:hKsh1} and \eqref{axiom:hKsh2}
conclusions: the canonical map $H^{\bullet}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \check{H}^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F}^{\bullet})$ is an isomorphism
nodes.label: prop:homotopy_k_sheaf_compute_chech

nodes.name: Čech cohomology vanishes when stalks vanish
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves that verify \eqref{axiom:Ksh3} and such that all the stalks are $0$ then $\check{H}^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F})=0$
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves that verify \eqref{axiom:Ksh3}
all the stalks are $0$
nodes.label: lem:chech_is_determined_by_stalks_1

nodes.name: Čech cohomology vanishes when stalks are acyclic
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves that verify \eqref{axiom:hKsh3} and $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}=0$ for $i<<0$. Then if the stalks of $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ are acyclics, $\check{H}^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F}^{\bullet})=0$
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a complex of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves that verify \eqref{axiom:hKsh3} and $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}=0$ for $i<<0$.
the stalks of $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ are acyclics
nodes.label: lem:chech_is_determined_by_stalks_2

nodes.name: Čech cohomology is determined by stalks
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ and $\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ be complexes of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves that verify \eqref{axiom:hKsh3} and $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}=H^i\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}=0$ for $i$ small enough. Then if a morphism $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ induces a quasi-isomorphism on stalks, $\check{H}^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{F}^{\bullet})=\check{H}^{\bullet}(X;\mathcal{G}^{\bullet})$
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ and $\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ be complexes of $\mathcal{K}$-presheaves that verify \eqref{axiom:hKsh3} and $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}=H^i\mathcal{G}^{\bullet}=0$ for $i$ small enough.
a morphism $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}\to \mathcal{G}^{\bullet}$ induces a quasi-isomorphism on stalks
nodes.label: prop:chech_is_determined_by_stalks_3

nodes.name: Pure homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf
nodes.statement: A homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ is said to be pure on $X$ if: \begin{itemize} \item For $p\in X$ and $i\neq 0$, $(H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet})_p=0$ \item $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}=0$ for $i<<0$ locally on $X$: ie for all $p\in X$ there is an open neighbourhoud $U$ of $p$ and an integer $N$ such that for $i\leq N$ and $K\subset U$: $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(K)=0$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf whose cohomology stalks vanish outside degree 0 and whose cohomology vanishes locally in sufficiently negative degrees.
nodes.label: def:pure_homotopy_k_sheaf

nodes.name: Consequences of purity
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a pure-homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf. Then: \begin{itemize} \item For $i<0$ $H^i\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}=0$ \item $H^0\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ is a $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf. \end{itemize}
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a pure-homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf.
nodes.label: lem:csq_of_pure_homotopy_k_sheaf

nodes.name: Cohomology of pure homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves is Čech cohomology of $H^0$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a pure-homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf. Then there is a canonical isomorphism: \[H^{\bullet}\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}(X)=\check{H}^{\bullet}(X;H^0\mathcal{F}^{\bullet})\]. More generaly: Let $[\mathcal{F}_0^{\bullet}\to \ldots\mathcal{F}_n^{\bullet-n}]$ be a complex of pure-homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves, then there is a canonical isomorphism: \[H^{\bullet}[\mathcal{F}_0^{\bullet}(X)\to \ldots\mathcal{F}_n^{\bullet-n}(X)]=\check{H}^{\bullet}(X;[H^0\mathcal{F}_0^{\bullet}\to\ldots\to (H^0\mathcal{F}_n^{\bullet})[n]])\]
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a pure-homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf.
Let $[\mathcal{F}_0^{\bullet}\to \ldots\mathcal{F}_n^{\bullet-n}]$  be a complex of pure-homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves
Let $\mathcal{F}^{\bullet}$ be a pure-homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaf.
Let $[\mathcal{F}_0^{\bullet}\to \ldots\mathcal{F}_n^{\bullet-n}]$  be a complex of pure-homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves

nodes.statement_short: For pure homotopy $\mathcal{K}$-sheaves, global cohomology equals Čech cohomology of $H^0$, also for total complexes of such.
nodes.label: prop:cech_of_pure_homotopy_k_sheaf
